did_you_know.text: Did you know? In his vision, Amos sees a “basket of summer fruit.” This vision introduces the prophecy of disaster in the chapter.

Did you know? The vision of the summer-fruit basket contains a play on the Hebrew words for “summer fruit” and “the end”: just as summer fruit has ripened, the LORD announces that the end has come for Israel.
Did you know? Amos describes a dramatic reversal: the songs of the temple will become wailing, and instead of joy there will be profound mourning, with corpses everywhere and silence reigning—“Hush!”
Did you know? The prophet addresses those who trample on the poor and seek to eliminate the needy of the land—a direct condemnation of social and economic injustice.

Did you know? The merchants described in the chapter wait for the month and the Sabbath to end so they can resume trading. Then they plan to make the ephah smaller, the shekel heavier, and the scales dishonest.
Did you know? Commercial corruption reaches its lowest point: the merchants want to buy the poor for next to nothing—even “for a pair of sandals”—and sell them refuse mixed in with good grain.
Did you know? The people’s sins are described as causing the land to tremble and mourn. The land will rise and sink and be swept along like the waters of the Nile in Egypt.
Did you know? One of the chapter’s images of disaster is the sun being darkened at noon—turning the time of light and clarity into a time of darkness.

Did you know? Amos describes a complete reversal of national joy: the festivals will become mourning, the songs will become laments, and the people will wear sackcloth and shave their heads as signs of mourning.

Did you know? The chapter describes a different kind of famine: not a famine of bread or a thirst for water, but a hunger to hear the word of the LORD. People will search throughout the land for the word of the LORD—but they will not find it.
